title: Chuang Tzu, Mystic, Moralist and Social Reformer
author: Chuang Tzu (Giles trans)
description: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, translated from the Chinese by Herbert A. Giles (London: Bernard Quaritch, 1889; revised 1926), the first complete English translation of the Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu, c. 369-286 BCE) is, with Laozi, the founding figure of philosophical Taoism. The work's thirty-three chapters combine philosophy, parable and humour: the giant Peng bird, Cook Ding carving the ox, the useless tree, the frog in the well, the debate on the happiness of fish, Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly, and his drumming and singing at his wife's death. Its teaching celebrates spontaneity, the relativity of all perspectives, the equality of things, the free and easy wandering of the sage, and acceptance of death and change in harmony with the Tao. Giles's introduction and notes present Zhuangzi as a critic of Confucian moralism. It is a primary text for Taoist mysticism and later Chan and Zen.
